scenes.visual: THE WORLD, kept for both films (16:9, dark navy background). Pale morph (typica) = warm CREAM moth; dark morph (carbonaria) = CHARCOAL moth with a thin white outline; birds = one simple BLUE bird silhouette; wasps (second film) = ORANGE. Every fitness axis is labelled 'relative fitness'. The word 'morph' is used on screen, never 'form' or 'type'. Cartoons and labelled blocks only; anything not computed carries a small 'schematic' tag. Same palette as the first film: wasps ORANGE, birds BLUE. Title card 'Two Enemies, One Gall' fades in over a goldenrod stem bearing one round gall.

scenes.tts: In the first film, birds made one moth morph survive better than the other. Now take a gall. If wasps attack small galls and birds attack large ones, which gall is safest?
scenes.visual: A quick echo of the first film's dial beside the moths, then it shrinks away. A tall goldenrod stem with a round gall swells up. On-screen question: 'Which gall is safest?' An ORANGE wasp icon at left, a BLUE bird icon at right.
scenes.narration: In the first film, birds made one moth morph survive better than the other. Now take a gall. If wasps attack small galls and birds attack large ones, which gall is safest?

scenes.tts: The goldenrod gall fly lays an egg in a bud of tall goldenrod. The plant grows a round gall around the larva. The larva spends the winter inside. The gall is made by insect and plant together, and galls vary widely in size.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of a gall showing a small larva inside. Then a dozen galls of very different diameters pop up in a scatter.
scenes.narration: The goldenrod gall fly lays an egg in a bud of tall goldenrod. The plant grows a round gall around the larva. The larva spends the winter inside. The gall is made by insect and plant together, and galls vary widely in size.

scenes.tts: Line the galls up by size, small on the left, large on the right. Above them we will draw relative fitness. That is how well larvae in galls of each size survive, compared with the average. A point above the dashed line means better than average.
scenes.visual: The galls slide into a row along a horizontal axis labelled 'gall size', small to large. An empty vertical axis labelled 'relative fitness' rises above the row, with a dashed line at 1 marked 'average'. Below the row, a wide bell-shaped histogram labelled 'gall sizes before'.
scenes.narration: Line the galls up by size, small on the left, large on the right. Above them we will draw relative fitness. That is how well larvae in galls of each size survive, compared with the average. A point above the dashed line means better than average.

scenes.tts: From the left come the wasps. A parasitoid develops on or in a host and ultimately kills it. This parasitoid wasp attacks larvae in small galls more than in large ones. Many small galls go dark.
scenes.visual: ORANGE wasps fly in from the left and land mostly on the small galls, a few on mid-size ones. Attacked galls dim to grey; survivors stay lit.
scenes.narration: From the left come the wasps. A parasitoid develops on or in a host and ultimately kills it. This parasitoid wasp attacks larvae in small galls more than in large ones. Many small galls go dark.

scenes.tts: From the right come the birds. Birds more often peck open the large galls and take the larva inside. Many large galls go dark too.
scenes.visual: BLUE birds swoop in from the right and peck open mostly the large galls. Those dim to grey. The middle-size galls stay brightest.
scenes.narration: From the right come the birds. Birds more often peck open the large galls and take the larva inside. Many large galls go dark too.

scenes.tts: So the middle survives best, with two named enemies pressing from opposite sides. Take a simple model where the two enemies are equally strong. The fitness curve rises, peaks over intermediate galls, and falls again. Favouring the middle over both extremes is called stabilizing selection. Below, the spread of gall sizes narrows.
scenes.visual: Points appear above each size class at heights read from the lit survivors, and a smooth curve draws through them: a symmetric hump. Corner tag 'schematic toy model: mirror-image attack curves, equal strength, survival from both enemies multiplied, symmetric starting sizes'. Label 'stabilizing'. The histogram below shrinks to a narrower bell centred in the same place (schematic example: the symmetric hump leaves the mean unchanged and reduces the spread; no numbers shown).
scenes.narration: So the middle survives best, with two named enemies pressing from opposite sides. Take a simple model where the two enemies are equally strong. The fitness curve rises, peaks over intermediate galls, and falls again. Favouring the middle over both extremes is called stabilizing selection. Below, the spread of gall sizes narrows.

scenes.tts: Now, in the model, make wasp attack heavier than bird attack. Does the average surviving gall stay in the middle?
scenes.visual: The ORANGE wasp icon grows larger; the BLUE bird icon stays the same. A vertical marker shows the old average gall size. On-screen: 'Does the average stay put?'
scenes.narration: Now, in the model, make wasp attack heavier than bird attack. Does the average surviving gall stay in the middle?

scenes.visual: Hold on the hump and the marker. A small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: No. In the model, the peak slides toward larger galls, away from the stronger enemy. The spread still narrows, but the average moves up. Favouring one end like this is directional selection. So one trait can carry a stabilizing and a directional component at once.
scenes.visual: The curve redraws as a chosen schematic example of heavier wasp attack (no numbers shown): the hump's peak sits right of the old-average marker. The histogram narrows and its centre shifts right; an arrow labelled 'mean moves up' points right. Two labels sit on the curve: 'stabilizing' (the hump) and 'directional' (the lean). Toy-model tag stays in the corner.
scenes.narration: No. In the model, the peak slides toward larger galls, away from the stronger enemy. The spread still narrows, but the average moves up. Favouring one end like this is directional selection. So one trait can carry a stabilizing and a directional component at once.

scenes.tts: A field study found this pattern in central Pennsylvania, across twenty fields over two years. Parasitoid attack was more frequent than bird attack in those fields. Intermediate galls survived best, and selection also favoured larger galls.
scenes.visual: A small map tag 'central Pennsylvania: 20 fields, 2 years' appears. The leaning hump stays on screen, tagged 'schematic: shape only'. No numbers shown.
scenes.narration: A field study found this pattern in central Pennsylvania, across twenty fields over two years. Parasitoid attack was more frequent than bird attack in those fields. Intermediate galls survived best, and selection also favoured larger galls.

scenes.tts: Now flip the hump into a dip. The middle does worst, and both ends do better. That shape is called disruptive selection. Theory predicts it when individuals crowd onto the commonest resource, and those that use something different do better.
scenes.visual: The curve inverts into a U-shaped dip, tagged 'schematic'. The histogram below thins in the middle and fattens at both ends. Label 'disruptive'. No organism shown.
scenes.narration: Now flip the hump into a dip. The middle does worst, and both ends do better. That shape is called disruptive selection. Theory predicts it when individuals crowd onto the commonest resource, and those that use something different do better.

scenes.tts: One end, the middle, or both ends. Directional, stabilizing and disruptive are shapes of one curve. They are not boxes a trait must fit. So read the curve first, then name the mode.
scenes.visual: Three small panels side by side: a rising line 'directional', a hump 'stabilizing', a dip 'disruptive', each with the 'relative fitness' axis. Then they slide together into one curve that morphs between the shapes.
scenes.narration: One end, the middle, or both ends. Directional, stabilizing and disruptive are shapes of one curve. They are not boxes a trait must fit. So read the curve first, then name the mode.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed row of galls, large white text, centred: 'The shape of the fitness curve names the mode of selection.'
